questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The record a cache poisoning attack abuses
questions.learningObjective: Explain which record a cache poisoning attack abuses
questions.stem: The brief asks why an attacker can poison a shared cache entry; explain the record that makes it possible.

answer.exemplar: The weakness is in how the cache decides what a response belongs to. If the key is built from only part of the request, such as the host and the path, then a header that the application reads but the key ignores lets an attacker choose the content that gets stored. The next visitor who produces the same key is served the attacker's response, which is why the record matters: it is what determines whether one client's answer can be handed to another client. A key that includes every input that changes the body removes the possibility entirely.

questions.explanation: The cache record is the key, and if it omits an input that changes the response, one client's answer is served to another. Keying on every input that affects the body removes that path.
questions.hint: The key decides who shares an answer.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The claim that completes a subdomain takeover
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a dangling host name is a design problem
questions.stem: The brief asks why a dangling host name is a design problem rather than an inconvenience; explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: The record carries an implicit promise that someone will honour it. Other systems, caches, certificates, bookmarks and partner integrations treat the name as a stable reference to a specific service, and they were built on the assumption that the record keeps pointing at the same operator. When the resource behind the name disappears but the record survives, that promise is broken and anyone able to claim the released name inherits the trust already built up around it. The problem is not tidiness, it is that a piece of routing metadata has become a transferable credential.

questions.explanation: Other systems treat the name as a stable reference, so a record surviving its resource turns routing metadata into a transferable claim on that trust. Untidiness is not the issue, inherited trust is.
questions.hint: Names carry trust, not just addresses.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The reconnaissance behind a targeted campaign
questions.learningObjective: Explain how reconnaissance shapes a targeted campaign
questions.stem: The brief asks why reconnaissance shapes a targeted campaign rather than just widening it; explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: Reconnaissance is valuable to a targeted campaign because it converts a generic capability into a specific one. Knowing which system processes a given type of request tells the attacker which payload will actually be executed instead of merely delivered. Knowing a named person's schedule tells them when that person will use a device the attacker can reach. Knowing a supplier's invoice workflow tells them which message thread to answer convincingly. Each of these removes a guess, and in a campaign where the target is one organisation, the number of guesses that must all go right falls sharply.

questions.explanation: Targeted reconnaissance removes specific guesses about system, person and workflow, so each step lands instead of merely arriving. Wider collection without that specificity adds noise, not accuracy.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The egress control that stops a server-side request forgery
questions.learningObjective: Explain why egress control beats input filtering
questions.stem: The brief asks why filtering the address a caller supplies is weaker than controlling outbound traffic; explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: Filtering the caller's string is a guess about what the fetch will actually do. The string can name a host that resolves differently inside the service's network than it does outside, can be rewritten by a redirect that the filter never sees, or can point at a numeric address form that no blocklist spelled out in words covers. Controlling outbound traffic removes the ambiguity instead of chasing it, because the destination that the service can actually reach is decided by the network rather than by the input. That is why egress policy, not input parsing, is the structural control.

questions.explanation: Filtering the input guesses the destination, while resolution, redirects and address forms can change it after the check. Egress policy decides where the service can reach, so it holds whatever the input says.
questions.hint: Decide where the service can reach.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The record a cache poisoning attack abuses
questions.learningObjective: Explain why cache poisoning is hard to contain
questions.stem: The brief asks why cache poisoning is harder to contain than a direct injection; explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: A direct injection affects the request that carried it, so the blast radius is the attacker and one response. A poisoned cache entry affects every later client whose request produces the same key, including clients who never spoke to the attacker and cannot be described as suspicious. Detection is correspondingly harder, because the malformed content arrives as a normal cached reply with a valid age and header set, and the origin logs show nothing unusual. Anyone who can influence a stored entry therefore gains an audience that grows without further effort from them.

questions.explanation: A poisoned entry is replayed to many clients with no link to the attacker, and it looks like an ordinary cached reply, so detection suffers. A direct injection touches only the request that carried it.

questions.learningObjective: Assess the value of a widely shared indicator
questions.stem: The brief examines an indicator that has appeared in 40 unrelated cases; which conclusion does the brief support?

The indicator is unusable, because a shared feature can never support any inference
options.misconception: overstates the weakness to prove nothing follows

options.text: The indicator proves a single state actor, because no criminal group shares tooling
options.misconception: invents exclusive use by one actor type

questions.explanation: An indicator appearing across many unrelated cases has little power to distinguish them, so its weight is low. That does not make it worthless or point to one actor, since groups share tooling freely.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The claim that completes a subdomain takeover
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a takeover exceeds a broken link
questions.stem: The brief asks why a takeover is more damaging than a broken link; explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: A broken link costs the organisation credibility and some traffic. A takeover costs it the trust that other parties extend to the name, and that trust is what other systems act on automatically. Partners who verify a webhook callback by name will send data to whatever answers. Certificate-based clients that pin the name will complete a handshake with the attacker. Search and mail records that were tied to the host now attach to new content, so even historic references can be redirected. The name keeps working, and it works for someone else, which is why the consequence is trust transfer rather than inconvenience.

questions.explanation: Other systems act on the name automatically, so a takeover redirects callbacks, pinned clients and historic references to the claimant. That is trust transfer, because the name keeps working for someone else.
questions.hint: The name keeps working, for them.

questions.explanation: The header is absent from the key but present in the origin's decision, so a stored response can carry the wrong language for later clients. The cache neither stops itself nor refuses requests.
questions.hint: The key missed the deciding input.

options.misconception: treats address notation as the only bypass

options.misconception: assumes writer validation neutralises both formats

options.text: Only the structured build is safe, because its format delimits fields without newlines

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The reconnaissance behind a targeted campaign
questions.learningObjective: Explain why targeting raises reconnaissance cost
questions.stem: The brief asks why a targeted campaign invests in reconnaissance that a broad campaign would not need; explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: A broad campaign sends the same message to many recipients and depends on volume, so its reconnaissance needs are shallow: a domain, a plausible pretext, a list. A targeted campaign has to succeed against one specific organisation, and each of those specifics has to be right, because a single wrong guess lets the target recognise the attempt. Reconnaissance is what removes the guesswork from those specific points, such as which person handles a particular kind of request, what a legitimate message from that supplier looks like, and when the target's mail system processes incoming mail. The effort looks disproportionate next to a spray, and that is exactly why it is spent.

questions.explanation: A targeted campaign must be right about one organisation, and reconnaissance removes the guesses that would expose it, while a broad campaign depends on volume and tolerates mistakes. The effort buys reliability.
questions.hint: Wrong guesses expose a targeted attempt.

questions.learningObjective: Specify handling when an identity cannot be validated
questions.stem: The brief asks how a service should treat a response whose identity cannot be validated; which two-part handling rule fits?

options.text: Fail closed and surface the failure to the operator, rather than retrying or degrading quietly
Retry the request immediately, because a second attempt usually returns the right identity
options.misconception: assumes retries fix a name mismatch

options.text: Accept the response but mark it untrusted, so each caller can decide for itself
options.misconception: delegates a security decision to every caller

options.text: Fall back to an unvalidated cached copy, which keeps the service available throughout

questions.explanation: If identity cannot be established, the safe behaviour is to stop and tell someone, because continuing means acting on an answer from an unknown source. Retrying or caching continue the risk.

options.misconception: relies on persistence rather than appearance

options.text: The entry is served to many clients, so nobody reports it as unusual
options.misconception: relies on volume of victims rather than appearance

options.misconception: describes changing content rather than concealment

options.text: The stored entry looks like an ordinary cached reply, complete with normal headers and age

questions.explanation: A poisoned entry is served with the headers, age and status a cache normally produces, so its appearance marks nothing as false. Persistence and volume explain other properties, not the concealment.
questions.hint: It looks like every other cached reply.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret the exposure created by a parsing disagreement
questions.stem: The brief counts 3,000 requests arriving at a proxy in a minute, of which 40 were forwarded with a body the origin parsed differently; which conclusion does the survey support?

options.text: Most requests were affected, because the 40 that differed represent the typical case
options.misconception: generalises from the minority to the majority

options.text: Only a small fraction was exposed to the disagreement, but each such request can affect the next
The disagreement had no effect, because only 40 requests were involved
options.misconception: concludes safety from a small count

options.text: The origin was overloaded, because 3,000 requests a minute exceeds its capacity
options.misconception: mistakes traffic volume for the parsing flaw

questions.explanation: A small fraction still matters, because a smuggled request is prepended to someone else's, so the effect is not confined to the 40 odd requests. Traffic volume says nothing about the flaw.
questions.hint: One bad request affects the next.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The egress control that stops a server-side request forgery
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an allow list beats a blocklist
questions.stem: The brief asks why an egress allow list is preferred over blocking known internal addresses; explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: A blocklist of internal addresses works only against the addresses someone remembered to write down, and the space of internal targets is larger than any such list: new services, cloud metadata endpoints in each provider's own ranges, and services reachable only on some deployments. An allow list works in the opposite direction, because it names what the service is allowed to reach, and anything unnamed is unreachable by default. That direction matters when the list of things to protect is open-ended but the list of things the service legitimately needs is small and known.

questions.explanation: An allow list names what the service may reach, so anything new or forgotten stays unreachable by default, while a blocklist depends on enumerating every internal target. Legitimate needs are few and known.
questions.hint: Name the permitted, not the forbidden.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The record a cache poisoning attack abuses
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a cache key should be derived
questions.stem: The brief asks why a cache key should be built from what the origin actually used; explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: A cache can only serve the right answer if it can tell answers apart. Every input the origin consults is a variable in the answer: a header that selects language, a parameter that selects a price, a header that selects a tenant's branding. If the key is built from the request fields that are convenient to read rather than from the ones the origin reads, two requests with different outcomes can produce the same key. The cache then has no way to know which answer belongs to which request, and it is not that the cache is wrong about anything, it is that it was asked a question with no single answer.

questions.explanation: The key must separate answers, so it must include every input the origin consults, not just convenient ones. Otherwise two outcomes share a key and the cache cannot tell which answer belongs to which request.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The claim that completes a subdomain takeover
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to design name records against takeover
questions.stem: The brief asks how a team should design name records so that they cannot be taken over; explain the principle and the practice.

answer.exemplar: The principle is that a name record should never point at a resource whose ownership can lapse while the record stays. In practice that means deciding who may hold each name and how that ownership is transferred, then recording the holder alongside the record rather than assuming it follows from the resource. Where a record must point at a shared or external service, the team keeps a check on the service's status and removes or repoints the record as soon as the service is retired. The habit that follows from this is simple: the removal of a resource and the removal of its name are one task, not two, and the second is not optional because it no longer serves a purpose.

questions.explanation: A record must not outlive the ownership behind it, so name retirement belongs to resource retirement and the holder is recorded explicitly. Assuming ownership follows the resource leaves the record claimable.

questions.learningObjective: Specify how a platform should treat an ambiguous request
questions.stem: The brief asks how a platform should treat a request that two of its own components parse differently; which two-part rule fits?

options.text: Let the front end's reading stand, because the front end is closest to the client
options.misconception: picks a side without a rule

options.text: Let the origin's reading stand, because the origin performs the sensitive action
options.misconception: picks a side without a rule

options.text: Accept the request under either reading, because a valid outcome in one view suffices
options.misconception: treats ambiguous parsing as harmless
